# u4-go

A Go port of *Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar* (1985, DOS), built on Ebiten. It is a
function-by-function translation of the decompiled C source of AVATAR.EXE and TITLE.EXE
([u4-decompiled](https://github.com/memmaker/u4-decompiled)), so the game rules, quirks and bugs
of the original are kept. See `PORTING.md` for the porting rules.

No original game data is included. Bring your own copy of the game (for example the GOG
release); the port reads its files at runtime. Nothing is ever written to the game directory.

## Build and run

Needs Go 1.26 or newer.

    go build -o u4 ./cmd/u4
    ./u4 -import /path/to/your/game     # once: copies the game files into ./data
    ./u4                                # play

`-import SRC` takes a plain folder, a zip, a CD image (ISO/BIN/CUE), a GOG installer
(`setup_*.exe`/`.bin`) or loose files, finds the game files in it and exits.

Flags:

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `-data DIR` | game files directory (default `data`) |
| `-save DIR` | saved games directory (default `save`) |
| `-import SRC` | import the game from SRC into `-data`, then exit |
| `-scale N` | window scale (default 3) |
| `-ega` | start with the original EGA graphics instead of the VGA upgrade |
| `-nomusic` | no MIDI music |

The layout is goplay's: run from the binary's directory, it needs no flags. Music is
synthesised from the GeneralUser GS SoundFont at `../../system/sf2/GeneralUser-GS.sf2`
(`tools/fetch-soundfont.sh` fetches it for the tests), and the music and effect volumes come
from goplay's `../../settings.toml`.

## Controls

The original keys work as in the DOS game. In addition:

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| Enter / right click | command menu (pauses the game) |
| Click on the map | walk there |
| F1 | help |
| F2 | toggle EGA / VGA graphics |
| F3, F4 | overlays |
| F5 | message history |
| F6 | original screen layout |
| Alt-V, Alt-+/Alt-- | music on/off, volume |

The modern view is wider than the original 11x11 map; game rules are unchanged, and menu
entries only queue the original keys.

## Layout

- `cmd/u4`: entry point
- `internal/u4`: AVATAR.EXE port, one Go file per C module
- `internal/title`: TITLE.EXE port
- `internal/host`, `internal/ega`, `internal/speaker`, `internal/music`: display, input and sound
- `internal/gamefs`, `internal/gameimport`: game file lookup and `-import`
- `internal/goplay`: the goplay launcher's settings and shared system folder

## Status

| Part | State |
|------|-------|
| Title / intro | ported |
| Avatar (world, towns, dungeons, combat) | ported |
| Sound and MIDI music | working |
| Wide view, menus, VGA upgrade | working |

Run the tests with `go test ./...`.

## Legal

Ultima is a trademark of Electronic Arts. This project is unaffiliated and ships no game assets.

# EDPACK in Rust

A modern re-implementation of **EDPACK** ("Editor de Aventuras Gráficas", José Luis Serrano
Moreno, 1990s), the Spanish DOS toolkit for point-and-click graphic adventures. It plays the
games made with the DOS versions natively, both EDPACK v1 (`RUNVGA.EXE`) and EDPACK v2.0x
(`RUNDAT.EXE`, shareware and registered runtimes), and it replaces the v2 DOS-only toolchain.

It is based on the shareware versions of the Editor de Aventuras Gráficas (EDPACK), which were
distributed for free on Spanish magazine cover CDs: v2.0 on *Micromanía* CD 35 (folder `ED`), and
v2.02 on *PCManía* issue 67 (May 1998), in the folder `sharewar\varios\edpack20`
([ISO image](https://archive.org/download/PCMCDS/PCMania%20CD67_1.iso)). The EDPACK v1 demo is on
*Micromanía* CD 21 (folder `EDPACK`).

| Original (DOS) | Replacement | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `RUNDAT.EXE` | `edpack` | Plays a packed `EDGAME.DAT` |
| `RUNFILES.EXE` | `edpack <folder>` | Plays compiled `NIVEL.*` files (or `.ED` sources, compiled on the fly) |
| `ED.EXE` | `edc <src> <out>` | Compiles `.ED` sources to `NIVEL.*` |
| `ED2DAT.EXE` | `edc <src> <out> --pack` | Packs a game into `EDGAME.DAT` |
| `SBFMDRV.COM`, `CT-VOICE.DRV` | `src/audio/` | OPL2 FM emulator for CMF music, VOC playback |
| `RUNVGA.EXE` (EDPACK v1) | `edpack <folder>` | Plays a v1 `RESOURCE.DAT` (or `<base>.nnn` files) |

Games known to work, each played to its ending by the test suite:

| Game | Made with | Interpreter |
|---|---|---|
| *Peter's Adventure I* (the demo) | EDPACK v2.0 shareware | `RUNDAT.EXE` v1.0 shareware |
| *Peter's Adventure I*, *PCManía* 67 build | EDPACK v2.02 shareware | `RUNDAT.EXE` v1.03 shareware |
| *El Dios de Nauru* (BYK Software, 2001) | EDPACK v2.03 | `RUNDAT.EXE` v1.0 registered |
| *Dadton Aguinández* (Coctel Software, 1998) | EDPACK v2.02 | `RUNDAT.EXE` v1.02 |
| *Las Aventuras de Manolo Kabezabolo* (Digital Legion, 1997) | EDPACK v1 | `RUNVGA.EXE` v1.03 |
| The EDPACK v1 demo (Omega Works, 1996) | EDPACK v1 | `RUNVGA.EXE` v1.0 |

The variant is detected from the data. See [`docs/history.md`](docs/history.md)
for the versions; the Windows rewrite EDPACK 2000 is a different program and is not supported.

The engine was built by reverse-engineering the original interpreter. The EDPACK package comes
with a demo game, *Peter's Adventure I*, both compiled (`EDGAME.DAT`) and as `.ED` sources. No
EDPACK files or games are included in this repository; get them from the CD image above.

## Building

You need Rust (stable). On Linux you also need the ALSA development headers for sound
(`sudo apt install libasound2-dev`). The window uses X11 (works under XWayland).

```sh
cargo build --release
```

To make `edpack` play a game when started without arguments, name its `EDGAME.DAT` at build
time:

```sh
EDPACK_DEMO_DAT=/path/to/EDGAME.DAT cargo build --release
```

## Playing

```sh
target/release/edpack game/EDGAME.DAT   # any EDPACK game
target/release/edpack game              # a folder: EDGAME.DAT, NIVEL.* files, .ED sources or a v1 RESOURCE.DAT
target/release/edpack                   # the game embedded at build time, if any
```

Options:

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--scale N` | Window size: 320×240×N (4:3) |
| `--speed 0-4` | Game speed (default: the game's SETUP.CFG, else 2) |
| `--text-speed 0-4` | Text speed (default: the game's SETUP.CFG, else 3) |
| `--mute` | No sound |
| `--saves DIR` | Where savegames go (default `~/.local/share/edpack/<title>/SAVEGAME._N_`) |

The controls are those of the original:

| Input | Action |
|---|---|
| Left click | Act |
| Right click | Cycle the verb: *Ir a*, *Mirar*, *Coger*, *Usar*, *Hablar* |
| Mouse to the top edge | Open the inventory. *Usar* on an object picks it up, then use it on something. |
| Space | Load / save / quit menu |
| Ctrl+C | Quit |

EDPACK v1 games have no verbs. Left click on a thing does what that thing is set up for (look at it,
use it, go there); right click takes it. The inventory is the bar at the bottom: left click on an
object describes it, right click picks it up to use on a thing or on another object. Ctrl+Esc
quits, as in the original.

## Tools

```sh
target/release/edc src out --pack                    # ED.EXE + ED2DAT.EXE
target/release/edc src out --pack --v202             # ED.EXE v2.02's formats (RUNDAT v1.03)
target/release/edc FUENTES out --pack --chain ROOM4.ED,ROOM2.ED,ROOM0.ED,ROOM1.ED,ROOM3.ED,ROOM5.ED
                                                     # rebuilds the demo's shipped EDGAME.DAT exactly
target/release/edtool run EDGAME.DAT shots tests/walkthrough/peter.txt   # headless play + PNGs
target/release/edtool disasm EDGAME.DAT 3            # decompile level 3's scripts
target/release/edtool dump EDGAME.DAT                # summary of every level
target/release/edtool cmf2wav SATAIR.CMF satair.wav
cargo test --release                                 # unit and end-to-end tests
```

The end-to-end tests need the games, which are not part of this repository; keep them elsewhere
and point the tests at them with environment variables. For the demo, give its compiled
`EDGAME.DAT` and the folder with its sources:

```sh
EDPACK_DEMO_DAT=/path/to/DEMO/EDGAME.DAT EDPACK_DEMO_SRC=/path/to/FUENTES cargo test --release
```

They play the demo to the end three ways: from the original `EDGAME.DAT`, from the sources, and
from an `EDGAME.DAT` built by `edc --pack`. They check that all three runs end at the same
simulated moment. The compiler's output is checked byte for byte against what the original ED.EXE
and ED2DAT.EXE produce (run in DOSBox, `tools/re/README.md`), and the demo's shipped `EDGAME.DAT`
is rebuilt from its sources byte for byte.

The *PCManía* 67 build of the demo is tested with `EDPACK_DEMO103_DAT` (its `EDGAME.DAT`) and
`EDPACK_DEMO103_SRC` (its `FUENTES` folder, compiled and compared byte for byte with the original
ED.EXE v2.02, and rebuilt into its shipped `EDGAME.DAT`).
Other games are played to their endings when given: `EDPACK_NAURU_DAT` and `EDPACK_DADTON_DAT`
name the `EDGAME.DAT` of *El Dios de Nauru* and *Dadton Aguinández*, and `EDPACK_MANOLO` the folder with the `RESOURCE.DAT` of *Las Aventuras
de Manolo Kabezabolo* (EDPACK v1), and `EDPACK_V1DEMO` the folder of the EDPACK v1 demo. Tests whose variables are not set are skipped.

For debugging, `EDPACK_SNAPSHOT=<seconds>:<file.png> edpack ...` saves the window after that
many seconds and quits.

## How it works

- **Memory model** (`memory.rs`). Script variables are pointers into the interpreter's global
  data, and many of them overlap byte fields (writing variable 31 also clears variable 30, and
  so on). The engine keeps its state in a 64 KiB array laid out like the original DS segment, so
  these side effects happen exactly as in DOS.
- **Formats** (`dat.rs`, `level.rs`, `specials.rs`, `font.rs`, `pcx.rs`, `fli.rs`). Supported:
  - `EDGAME.DAT`: offset table; resources are stored +5.
  - Compiled levels: a 30-byte header followed by RLE blocks of fixed-size tables.
  - NIVEL.INV, NIVEL.MOV, NIVEL.MOU, NIVEL.IAC, NIVEL.TIT.
  - EDLETRAS fonts, PCX, Autodesk FLI, CMF, VOC.

  Strings are obfuscated with a different key per kind of string.
- **Engine threading** (`host.rs`, shared by both engines). The original is a blocking DOS program: a main loop that
  waits two VGA retraces per pass (about 28.5 ms), a 50 Hz timer interrupt, and routines with
  their own loops (fades, FLI playback, menus). The engine keeps that structure and runs on its
  own thread. Whenever time must pass it hands the frame to the host and waits for the clock to
  advance. Host and engine never run at the same time, so play is deterministic for a given
  input sequence.
- **Interpreter** (`Engine::run_script`). A port of the bytecode interpreter: 66 opcodes, an
  8-bit program counter, and arguments ≥ 25000 dereferenced as variables. `DELAY` keeps its
  counter inside the bytecode, and the 51-operation runaway check is kept.
- **Player** (`player.rs`). Path planning follows the original: LIMIT redirection, then the
  three-pass LIMITMOV rule search. It also covers the walker with its frame rules, the float32
  nearest-neighbour downscaler, SCALEMOV/SHADOWMOV, and layer swapping.
- **UI** (`ui.rs`, `menu.rs`). Speech layout and timing, the info bar, STEXT dialogue choices,
  the inventory panel, object combination (ACINVINV) and use-on-thing (ACINVTH), and the
  load/save menu.
- **Compiler** (`compiler/`). The `.ED` parser, script lowering, and the LIMITMOV rule
  generator. Scripts, LIMITMOV tables, texts, doors and the MOV/MOU/IAC/TIT files are identical
  to what the original ED.EXE produced for the demo.
- **v2 runtime variants** (`level.rs`, `dat.rs`). The registered archives have 1000 level slots,
  the registered level files lack the shareware's filler bytes, and RUNDAT v1.02 has 12-byte
  animation records, a skip key (ASLT/DSLT), PUTXY/SEEANIM, a 200-operation limit and some UI changes. The
  layout is detected by parsing the levels each way. Details: `docs/v2-rundat/07-versions.md`.
- **EDPACK v1** (`v1/`). A separate engine for RUNVGA.EXE: its own data segment layout, the raw
  level tables of `RESOURCE.DAT`, the 41-opcode interpreter, the walker, the verbless click
  logic, the inventory bar, texts, the incremental screen updates and the SPACE menu. Details:
  `docs/v1-runvga/`.

Some quirks of the original are reproduced on purpose, because games were tested against them:

- `SEEINV` always returns 0.
- `NEWMOUSE` uses a 60-byte stride, so only cursor set 0 loads correctly.
- `DELAY(n)` with large counts can end the script early.
- `ACTION(n)` restarts the calling script.
- The info bar picks the first thing in draw order, not the topmost one.

Some things are deliberately different:

- There is no shareware level limit. Shareware archives (6 level slots) do show the shareware
  runtime's start-up notice: 6 seconds, or until a key is pressed.
- Savegames use their own file format.
- The screen is redrawn completely on every pass instead of with dirty rectangles.
- FM music comes from an emulator.
- Fades run at a fixed speed. The original's fade speed depended on the CPU.

The documentation is in [`docs/`](docs/README.md): the EDPACK versions and the games known to use
them ([`docs/history.md`](docs/history.md)), and the reverse-engineering specs of both interpreters
([`docs/v1-runvga/`](docs/v1-runvga/), [`docs/v2-rundat/`](docs/v2-rundat/)).

## License

programs or the games made with them, such as the demo, which belong to their authors.

# frontier-decompile

Research toward a 1:1, cross-platform, browser-capable (WASM) reimplementation of
**Frontier: Elite II** (DOS, 1993) in Rust + wgpu, done in the same way as the
[Banished reimplementation](https://github.com/tanepiper/banished-decompile).

This repository contains **no game code and no game assets**. It holds format documentation, tooling
and, over time, an engine reimplementation. To use it you need your own copy of the game. The tools
copy the original files from your install into local, git-ignored folders.

## Layout

| Path | Contents | In git? |
|---|---|---|
| `docs/` | Reverse-engineering findings and format specs | yes |
| `tools/` | Asset copy script, DOSBox reference runner, Ghidra scripts | yes |
| `crates/`, `apps/` | The Rust reimplementation | yes |
| `game-data/original/` | Read-only copy of your `FRONTIER.EXE`, `EL2*.OVL` and data files | **no** |
| `game-data/run/` | Writable copy that DOSBox runs (saved games land here) | **no** |
| `game-data/derived/` | Captures, emulator dumps, exported images | **no** |
| `analysis/` | Ghidra project and decompiled output | **no** |

## Getting started

Requirements: Rust (stable, with `rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo install trunk`
for the web build later), and DOSBox Staging (`brew install dosbox-staging`) to run the original.
For analysis you also need Ghidra 12.1.x and JDK 21 (`brew install ghidra`). The REA MCP server
(the `reverse-engineer-anything` skill) uses the same Ghidra install.

```bash
# 1. Copy your game into game-data/ (read-only original + DOSBox working copy)
FRONTIER_DIR=/path/to/frontier tools/extract-assets.sh

# 2. Run the original game as the reference
tools/dosbox/run.sh
tools/dosbox/reset.sh            # throw away saves/state in game-data/run

# 3. Ghidra analysis of FRONTIER.EXE and every overlay into analysis/export (~20 s)
tools/ghidra/export.sh

# 4. The game (native window; runs your original files on the reference runtime) and tests
cargo run --release -p frontier-app
cargo test --release             # the game-data tests skip if game-data/ is missing

# 5. The game in the browser (WASM; your files are served only to 127.0.0.1)
tools/dev-web.sh                 # http://127.0.0.1:8743/?data=/game-data/

# 6. The resource viewer: every file, picture, song, model and string in your copy
cargo run --release -p frontier-viewer [-- path/to/game]
tools/dev-web.sh --app viewer    # http://127.0.0.1:8741/?data=/game-data/
```

### The resource viewer

`frontier-viewer` (`apps/viewer`) browses your own game files outside the game, natively or in the
browser (pick the files, or `?data=` from the dev server). It shows the MZ headers, relocations,
overlay export blocks and module headers of the program and every overlay; the 225 pictures of
`EL2G.GRF` and the `PIC000.GRF` screenshot; the `.ROL` MIDI songs (tracks and events, with an OPL2
approximation to listen to); the AdLib songs and effects, played by the ported original driver;
the 3D models of both model tables, drawn and listed command by command; the strings of every
binary; and a hex view for the packed position files and anything not yet understood. Formats and
how each is known: [docs/FORMATS.md](docs/FORMATS.md).

| Crate | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `crates/formats` | Dependency-free readers for the shipped files: MZ images, overlay headers, `.GRF` pictures and screenshots, MIDI, 3D models, text ([docs/FORMATS.md](docs/FORMATS.md)) |
| `crates/platform` | Host services both apps share: the audio output (cpal / WebAudio), loading the player's files (a folder, `?data=`, the file picker) and the browser page glue |
| `crates/opl` | YM3812 (OPL2) FM chip at its native 49,716 Hz, and the band-limited resampler for the audio output ([docs/AUDIO.md](docs/AUDIO.md)) |
| `crates/hooks` | Installs native ports at the original routines' addresses; parity tests and shadow verification ([docs/MATH3.md](docs/MATH3.md)) |
| `crates/dos` | Reference runtime: 386 real-mode CPU + DOS/BIOS/EMS/VGA services that run the original as oracle and scaffold ([docs/RUNTIME.md](docs/RUNTIME.md)) |
| `crates/game` | Deterministic game logic, ported 1:1 and proven bit-exact against the original |
| `apps/game` | `frontier`: the game, native and browser |
| `apps/viewer` | `frontier-viewer`: the resource viewer, native and browser |

## Status

See [docs/FINDINGS.md](docs/FINDINGS.md) for what is known about the binaries and the milestone plan.

- [x] M0: reference runtime (DOSBox Staging), repository layout, Ghidra export
- [x] Playable: the original runs on the in-process runtime, native and WASM, from boot through the
  intro and start menu into the cockpit ([docs/RUNTIME.md](docs/RUNTIME.md)); native ports replace it
  routine by routine
- [x] Audio: the AdLib driver is ported natively and plays the original music and effects
  through an OPL2 model. Its audio is identical sample for sample to the original driver's. One
  stereo output natively (cpal) and in the browser (WebAudio) ([docs/AUDIO.md](docs/AUDIO.md)).
  A DOSBox audio comparison remains
- [x] Video: all 40 `EL2MCGA3` exports (polygons flat and textured, lines, discs, the model and
  scanline fills, text, bitmaps with their EMS cache, the palette and the flip) are ported
  natively; shadow-verified over 90 s of play with 0 mismatches, frames identical to the original
  ([docs/VIDEO.md](docs/VIDEO.md))
- [ ] M1: function discovery across `FRONTIER.EXE` and the overlays; overlay loader traced
  (loader and seeding done, see [docs/OVERLAYS.md](docs/OVERLAYS.md); indirect calls and names remain)
- [ ] M2: data formats. `EL2G.GRF` and the screenshot format, the MIDI songs, the model tables,
  headers and vertices decoded, and every model's command list walked (lengths measured on the
  runtime); ships, stations and starports named and drawn in the resource viewer; saved commanders and the position files remain ([docs/FORMATS.md](docs/FORMATS.md))
- [ ] M3: boot flow and intro rendered by the reimplementation
- [ ] M4: maths core (fixed point, RNG) and galaxy/system generation, bit-exact. All 47 `EL2MATH3`
  routines (float arithmetic, square roots, rotation matrices, frame set-up, perspective projection,
  the model vertex transformer, face shading, 64-bit positions) ported and verified, running natively in the game with frames identical to the
  original over 60 s ([docs/MATH3.md](docs/MATH3.md))
- [ ] M5: flight, orbits and combat
- [ ] M6: stations, trade, missions, save/load

## Legal

Frontier: Elite II is © Frontier Developments / David Braben. This project is an independent,
non-commercial interoperability effort, not affiliated with or endorsed by the rights holders. Do not
commit or distribute game files, extracted assets or decompiled code.

cebion-balloonchallenge-decomp-readme-md.text:
# Balloon Challenge port

An unofficial port of **Balloon Challenge v2.0** (William Soleau / Soleau Software, 1993-1995), a DOS strategy
game, to Linux with SDL2.

The port runs the original DOS program, translated to native code by a static recompiler, on a runtime that
reproduces the PC it ran on (EGA, PC speaker, timer, keyboard, DOS and BIOS). Its behaviour is verified to
be 1:1 with the original: recorded play sessions are replayed in the original under DOSBox-X and in the port,
and screens, game state and speaker output are compared at every key press.

This repository contains no game files and no code derived from the game's program; the build generates
everything from the shareware `BALLOONC.EXE`. See `NOTICE.md` for what belongs to whom.

## Requirements

- Linux, CMake 3.16 or newer, a C++17 compiler, SDL2 development files.
- Python 3 with `iced-x86` and `unicorn` (`pip install --user iced-x86 unicorn`).
- [deark](https://entropymine.com/deark/) 1.7 or newer (unpacks the PKLITE and EXEPACK layers of the EXE).
- The shareware release `ballon20.zip` (e.g. from classicdosgames.com),
  sha256 `99b71a805a759cdad2b7ed6121c1221934a5c3430d99223ee164055e10ae4fd0`.

## Build

```shell
scripts/prepare.sh /path/to/ballon20.zip
```

This copies the game files to `original/` (not tracked), checks that `BALLOONC.EXE` is the v2.0 shareware
program, unpacks it, rebuilds the reference machine from it, generates the recompiled program into
`recomp/gen/` and builds `recomp/build-rc/rc_play`. After changes, `recomp/regen.sh` regenerates and
rebuilds.

## Play

```shell
recomp/build-rc/rc_play --data original              # window
recomp/build-rc/rc_play --data original --fullscreen
```

The folder given with `--data` holds the game files; the game writes its own files there too. With the
files of the registered version in that folder the port runs in registered mode (two human players); a
registered `BALLOONC.OV2` also unlocks through the game's own check.

## Layout

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `recomp/` | build of the recompiled port: `regen.sh`, `CMakeLists.txt`, `entries.txt` (code entry points found by discovery runs), `host/` (SDL2 player, headless runner, game-file check) |
| `recomp/recompiler/` | the static recompiler (Python, iced-x86): MZ loading, code discovery, x86-16 to C++ translation, reference-machine tools, QuickBASIC pattern lifter |
| `recomp/runtime/` | the C++ runtime the recompiled program runs on: CPU state, DOS and BIOS services, EGA, PIT/PIC, PC speaker, native-procedure support |
| `reference/` | the reference machine at the program's entry (DOSBox-X, program area blanked) and its display and timer timing logs |
| `src/game/` | decompiled procedures (C++, checked call by call against the recompiled program); generated region and module files are not tracked |
| `sessions/` | recorded play sessions (key sequences) used for verification |
| `tools/` | lockstep verification, region and module generators, coverage report |
| `docs/` | decisions, decompilation ledger |
| `docs/` | `recompilation.md`, `decompilation.md`, `dosbox-x-timing.md`: how the recompiler, the verified decompilation and the timing model work |

## Verification (development)

- `tools/verify_sessions.sh NAME...`: replays `sessions/play/NAME.json` in the original under an
  instrumented DOSBox-X (`tools/dosbox/dosbox-x-rea-instrumentation.patch`, driven by `tools/dosbox/dbx_debug.py`;
  set `REA_DOSBOX` to its binary) and in the port, then
  compares every stop.
- `recomp/record.sh NAME [--registered]`: record a new session by playing.
- `rc_headless --verify-native`: runs the decompiled C++ and checks each call against the recompiled program
  (registers, flags, instruction count, memory, video, port writes); `tools/native_coverage.py` reports which
  units the sessions reached.

Verification status: all 11 recorded sessions in `sessions/play/` match the original at every stop (screens,
game state, BIOS data); speaker output is identical in 9 of 11, the other two differ at one note join (a
DOSBox-X scheduling effect, `docs/dosbox-x-timing.md`).

## License

The port's code: GPL-2.0-or-later (`LICENSE`). The game is not covered; see `NOTICE.md`.

AmiPixelShop

A modern, layer-based image editor for the Amiga.
Native AmigaOS 3.2 · RTG · written in C and 68k assembler

--- Everyone is talking about **PhotoCraft**-style image editing - full-featured layer editors are available on just about every platform today. Now the Amiga gets one too. AmiPixelShop is **not a port and nothing was reverse-engineered**. It is written from scratch, natively for the Amiga: plain **C and 68k assembler** - no Rust, no emulation layers, no runtime. It opens its own RTG screen and draws everything itself, tuned for speed up to 1920×1080. I am a professional art designer, and my goal is to rebuild the tools I use every day as faithfully as the Amiga allows. Development is done with the help of **Claude** (Anthropic). > **Early beta - testers wanted!** > There are certainly still plenty of bugs. Please report anything you find through > [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/radi7777/AmiPixelShop/issues) - every report helps. ## Features | | | |---|---| | **Layers** | Up to 64 layers, 25 blend modes, opacity & fill, locks, groups (pass through / isolated), multi-selection, drag & drop | | **Masks** | Layer and group masks (linked or unlinked), clipping masks | | **Non-destructive** | Adjustment layers (Levels, Curves, Hue/Saturation, ...), layer styles (Drop Shadow, Outer Glow, Stroke), live Properties panel | | **Painting** | Brush, Eraser, Clone Stamp, History Brush, Spot Healing, Blur/Sharpen/Smudge, Dodge/Burn, Gradient, Paint Bucket, Shapes | | **Selections** | Marquee, Lasso, Polygonal Lasso, Quick Selection, Magic Wand, Color Range, Grow, Similar, Feather, Expand/Contract | | **Type** | TrueType/OpenType text that stays editable - alignment, tracking, leading, anti-aliasing | | **Paths** | Pen tool with Bezier curves, Paths panel - make selection, fill, stroke; undoable and saved | | **Transform** | Free Transform, Distort, Perspective, Warp, Crop, Image/Canvas Size, Image Rotation, Trim, Reveal All | | **Filters** | Liquify, Gaussian, Box & Motion Blur, Unsharp Mask, Sharpen, Median, Add Noise, Emboss, Find Edges, High Pass, Mosaic | | **Workflow** | Undo/Redo with History panel and History Brush, multiple documents, Auto-Select move tool, customizable toolbar, tooltips | | **Amiga colors** | Reduce Colors with live preview: optimized palettes (24 bit, OCS 12 bit, MagicWB, grayscale), 2-256 colors, EHB, HAM6, HAM8, Floyd-Steinberg / Atkinson / ordered dithering; New Document presets for all classic Amiga screen modes | | **Files** | Native `.aps` (keeps everything), layered `.psd` import, IFF ILBM import and export (EHB, HAM, 24 bit, palette and mode kept), PNG, JPEG, plus all formats your datatypes can read | ## Requirements - **PiStorm** with Emu68 (JIT-emulated 68040 + FPU) - this is the target platform - *Maybe:* a real 68060 with FPU and RTG (untested, will be slow at high resolutions) - **AmigaOS 3.2** - **RTG** (Picasso96 / P96) with a 24 or 32 bit screen mode, 1024×600 up to 1920×1080 - 128 MB Fast RAM or more **Tested on:** Amiga 500 + PiStorm (Raspberry Pi 3A+, Emu68), AmigaOS 3.2.3, P96. Classic 68000-68030 machines and AGA/ECS screens are **not** supported. ## Getting started 1. Download the latest archive from [Releases](https://github.com/radi7777/AmiPixelShop/releases) (also on Aminet). 2. Unpack it, e.g. to `Work:`, and start `AmiPixelShop`. 3. Choose a screen mode on the first start. **Read the HTML Guide for instructions:** [`docs/Guide.html`](docs/Guide.html) - it is included in the archive and works in IBrowse, AWeb and Voyager. ## Building from source Cross-compiled on macOS/Linux with [bebbo's amiga-gcc](https://github.com/bebbo/amiga-gcc) and vasm: ```sh make # produces build/AmiPixelShop ``` Notes: compile with `-m68040 -m68881` and link with `-mcpu=68020 -m68881` (see `Makefile`) - otherwise the math library goes through the Amiga math libraries and clobbers the FPU registers. ## Reporting bugs Please open an [issue](https://github.com/radi7777/AmiPixelShop/issues) and include: - what you did and what happened - your setup: PiStorm model, Emu68 version, AmigaOS version, screen mode, RAM - a screenshot or the image, if possible ## License AmiPixelShop is released under the [MIT License](LICENSE). Third-party code: [stb](https://github.com/nothings/stb) (stb_image, stb_image_write, stb_truetype - Public Domain / MIT) and [zlib](https://zlib.net) (zlib License). Interface font: Open Sans (Apache License 2.0). AmiPixelShop is an independent project and is not affiliated with any other software or vendor. All trademarks belong to their respective owners.

# Citadel — Java / jMonkeyEngine port A port of the 1995 Amiga first-person shooter **Citadel** by Virtual Design, rebuilt in Java on [jMonkeyEngine](https://jmonkeyengine.org/). Every rule, table and data format comes from the original 68000 assembly rather than being reinvented; only the renderer is new. ![Two enemies in the first complex, LEVEL01A](docs/images/enemies.png) The original is a cell-based software renderer: a 64 × 64 grid of 1024-unit cells, walls drawn as textured trapezoids back to front from a precomputed visibility table, all integer arithmetic, output as chunky pixels and converted to five Amiga bitplanes. The port drops that rendering path entirely — jMonkeyEngine draws real 3D — and keeps what actually matters: the data formats and the game rules. ## Screenshots
The title screen, after the intro animation The server's menu, in its own font, over the hangar
MAPA, choosing the next complex to attack A column of skulls, a carved face and a first aid kit
The laboratory: each complex has its own texture set The sewers
The interference burst when a shot lands The original death picture
## Playing ### From a package `gradle :game:jpackage` builds a self-contained folder with its own Java runtime (see [Packaging](#packaging)). It holds no game data: on first start it offers to download the original data from [Amiga-Citadel](https://github.com/pawelmat/Amiga-Citadel), or to use a copy already on disk, and converts it once. ### From source Needs a JDK 21 toolchain and the original data, which is not part of this repository: check out Amiga-Citadel next to it, so that its `Code/` and `Data/` sit in `../Amiga-Citadel`, or point the build elsewhere with `-Poriginal=`. Gradle downloads jMonkeyEngine on first build. ```sh git clone https://github.com/pawelmat/Amiga-Citadel ../Amiga-Citadel gradle :tools:convert # convert the original data into build/assets gradle :game:run # start from the intro gradle :game:run --args=LEVEL05B # or straight into a level ``` Conversion has to run once before the game: textures and sounds come from `build/assets`, while level data is read straight out of the original `.MAP` files. ### Controls | key | action | |---|---| | mouse | turn | | `W` `S` / `A` `D` | walk / strafe | | `E`, right mouse button | use the wall you are facing | | left mouse button, `Ctrl` | fire | | `1` … `6`, `0` | pick a weapon, back to the bare hand | | `M` | automap | | `Z` | interference off | | `-` `+` | game pace | | `F5` / `F9` | save / load menu | The original's seven cheat codes work too; [PORTING.md](PORTING.md#the-cheat-codes) explains how they were recovered from the obfuscated tables. ## What works - **The world** — all 28 levels and all 8 complexes: walls, sliding doors, floors, ceilings, animated walls and columns, blood stains and plaques, items and both enemy species. - **Movement** follows the original rules, not a physics engine: the 307-unit player radius, clamp-after-move sliding, corner handling, blocking columns, and the energy it costs to walk into a wall. - **Doors and switches** — doors open as you approach and shut behind you; wall switches run their command lists; teleports dissolve the view with the original chaos table. - **Combat** — enemies roam, close in, respect line of sight and shoot back; weapons fire hitscan or real projectiles (fireballs, electricity, rockets that burst into fireballs), with ammunition, weapon wear and the per-species vulnerability mask. - **Inventory** — weapons, ammunition, keycards, first aid, speed boost, vodka, and the six warhead sections with their assembly gauge. - **Status panel** — the original panel with every widget where the engine puts it: energy, heart monitor and the exhaustion behind it, compass, weapon reveal, ammunition, ID cards, and the scrolling message line with the original texts. - **Campaign** — the intro, the title screen, the server's menu in the hangar, MAPA between complexes, the level sequence with the inventory carried across, the death sequence, and the victory card. - **Sound** — the 25 effects, positioned in the world for doors and enemies. - **Saves** — a five-slot menu over the original 768-byte `Savegame.DAT` format. Not done yet: the pushes that go with a hit (`sv_AddMove` and the `sv_LastMove` rebound). [PORTING.md](PORTING.md#state) keeps the full list. ## How it is built | module | contents | dependencies | |---|---|---| | `core` | data formats, level model, game rules | none | | `tools` | asset converter and inspectors | `core`, `java.desktop` | | `game` | jMonkeyEngine front end | `core`, `tools`, jME 3.9 | `core` has no dependency on jMonkeyEngine or on `java.desktop`, so the whole rule set runs headless. `gradle :core:test` exercises it against the shipped maps, including a random walk of 20 000 steps across five levels asserting the player never ends up on the far side of a shut door. The converter also writes a readable dump and an overview of every level into `build/assets/maps` — walls in white, doors in blue, switches in amber, columns in grey, items in green, enemies in red, the spawn as a blue square and the exit as a green one — which is how the decoding was checked against the game. Two things were not written down anywhere and had to be worked out: `.VIR` graphics are stored column-major with a 65-byte stride, and the colour index is bit-reversed into bits 3..7 of each byte because the chunky-to-planar macro consumes bit 7 first. Cell values index the engine's sprite tables 1-based. For verification without a window in the way, `gradle :game:shot` renders one frame to `build/shots` and exits: `-Plevel=LEVEL03C`, `-Pscreen=title|hangar|map|dead|victory`, `-Pat=x,y,angle`, `-Pcheat=HOTKISS`. Every screenshot on this page was made that way.
## Packaging ```sh gradle :game:jpackage # a self-contained folder in game/build/jpackage/Citadel gradle :game:jpackage -Ptype=msi # a Windows installer, which needs the WiX toolset ``` The result carries its own Java runtime and the game, but no game data: about 80 MB, most of it the runtime. Two things keep that from being twice the size — `--add-modules` so jlink strips the JDK down to what jME actually uses, and dropping the LWJGL natives for every platform except the one being built for. On first start the game asks whether to download the original data from [Amiga-Citadel](https://github.com/pawelmat/Amiga-Citadel) (pinned to the commit the port was checked against, about 20 MB), or to use a checkout already on disk. It then converts it once, and keeps the data, the converted assets and the save file in a per-user folder: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Citadel` on Windows, `~/Library/Application Support/Citadel` on macOS, `~/.local/share/citadel` elsewhere. Delete that folder to start over. ## Documentation - **[PORTING.md](PORTING.md)** — coordinate system, movement rules, every ported routine with the assembly labels it comes from, where the port deliberately departs from the original, and the current state. - **[tools/README.md](tools/README.md)** — every original data format, decoded, with the assembly label that proves each claim. ## Credits and licence Citadel is Copyright © 1995, 2022 Virtual Design. Original code by Kane of Suspect. Java and jMonkeyEngine port by **Guillaume Monet**. The original sources come from [pawelmat/Amiga-Citadel](https://github.com/pawelmat/Amiga-Citadel). This package is free to copy and use for non-commercial purposes under the terms of the **GNU GPL-3.0** licence; see [LICENSE](LICENSE). It comes with absolutely no warranty of any kind.

# Gloom — Java port

*Read this in [French](README_FR.md).*

A Java port of **Gloom** (Black Magic Software, Amiga 1995), the first Doom clone to ship on the
Amiga. The engine is rewritten **line by line from the original 68020 assembly**
([earok/GloomAmiga](https://github.com/earok/GloomAmiga)) — no emulator, no reinterpretation: the
Java code follows the asm instruction by instruction, and the `.s` sources stay the reference
whenever something is in doubt.

The original engine is a software rasteriser that "draws" its scene into a **copperlist**: one
colour-register poke per pixel, replayed to the screen by the Amiga copper. The port throws that
display path away — it renders into a plain RGB framebuffer — and keeps what matters: the memory,
the arithmetic, the data formats and the game rules, taken from the assembly rather than guessed
at again.

![Title screen](docs/img/ecran-titre.png)

Ported by **Guillaume Monet**.

---

## Two renderers, one simulation

A launcher offers two views at startup. They share **exactly** the same game code: the same
emulated 68k RAM, the same object lists, the same AI, the same campaign script. Only the display
changes.

| | **GLOOM CLASSIC** | **GLOOM REBIRTH** |
|---|---|---|
| rendering | the original rasteriser, ported | a real 3D scene (jMonkeyEngine) |
| internal resolution | 320 × 240 | the screen's own |
| what you get | pixel fidelity | dynamic lighting, shadows, bloom, mouselook |

| CLASSIC (2D) | REBIRTH (3D) |
|---|---|
| ![Gloom Classic](docs/img/classic-2d.png) | ![Gloom Rebirth](docs/img/rebirth-3d.png) |

The HUD, the menus and the story screens are the game's own, decoded from its own data (IFF
images, 7-plane Amiga font):

| In-game HUD | Story screen |
|---|---|
| ![HUD](docs/img/classic-hud.png) | ![Story screen](docs/img/ecran-histoire.png) |

Two variants of the rasteriser are ported: `gloom.s` (chunky, `focshft 6`, wide FOV) and `gloom2.s`
(planar/AGA, `focshft 7` + `castrots128`, the less distorted "Deluxe" projection). They share the
same rasteriser — only the focal length and the ray table differ.

---

## Porting decisions

### 68k RAM as a plain byte array

All of the game's memory is **one flat, big-endian 64 MB `byte[]`** (`gloom.Mem`). Registers
`d0-d7`/`a0-a6` become `int`s, and every access goes through typed helpers (`Mem.b/w/l`, `ub/uw`,
`wb/ww/wl`) that reproduce 68k byte order and arithmetic. `gloom.M68k` covers the rest (`swap`,
`muls/mulu`, `divs/divu`, sign extension, `.w` shifts).

This is what makes the line-by-line port possible: a struct from the asm stays at **the same
address and the same offset** it had originally, quirks included. And there are quirks — in Gloom,
`ob_nxvec` and `ob_lives` are the **same word** (`rs.w 0`), as are `ob_nzvec` and `ob_infra`. A
"clean" port would have split those fields and broken the game silently.

The safety net: `gradle checkLayout` checks every struct offset against the `.s` file. It has to
print `TOUT OK`.

### What is NOT ported: the hardware layer

The copper, the blitter, C2P, the Paula audio registers and the CIA interrupts have no useful
equivalent here. In their place sits a thin **host layer**: LWJGL 3 (GLFW/OpenGL/OpenAL) on PC,
the Android APIs on phones. The engine knows nothing about it.

The decoupling is real and measurable: out of the port's ~13,500 lines, only **four files** depend
on LWJGL (`host/Main`, `host/Display`, `host/Audio`, `rebirth/DesktopGlue`), and the Android APK
compiles the **same sources** as the desktop build, without a single duplicated line. Two
interfaces isolate the rest:

- `HostGlue` — the three things in the 3D view that aren't portable (cursor lock and framebuffer
  size via GLFW, PNG screenshot writing via AWT);
- `AudioBackend` — OpenAL on PC, `AudioTrack` on Android.

### Audio rebuilt the way Paula did it

Sound isn't handed off to some higher-level library. The samples are in Gloom's own format
(`[period][length in words][signed 8-bit PCM]`), and the **Paula period** gives the playback
frequency (`3546895 / period`). On Android the 4 DMA voices are replayed by hand, with a 16.16
fixed-point step and the same voice-allocation rules (a free one, else the least prioritary one,
else nothing) — then mixed with the music into a single stream.

The MED music (MMD0/MMD1) is a player written for this port: sequencer plus 4-voice mixer, the
original replayer being a non-portable 68k blob.

### One simulation behind both renderers

The 3D view isn't a second game. It **reads the world state out of the 68k RAM** every frame and
translates it into a jMonkeyEngine scene: walls extruded from the map's zones, the original sprites
as billboards (with the 8-direction frame selection), gore decals on the floor, blood drops as a
single mesh. The simulation runs on a fixed timestep (1/60 s), so gameplay keeps its speed whatever
the framerate is.

### Android: what measuring taught us

The port runs on a phone (measured on a Xiaomi: 60 fps in 2D, ~55 in 3D). Two non-obvious findings,
reached by instrumenting rather than guessing:

- **The 2D ran at half speed** because `lockCanvas()` hands back a *software* canvas: scaling the
  320 × 240 framebuffer up to fullscreen was happening on the CPU. `Surface.lockHardwareCanvas()`
  was all it took (35 → 60 fps).
- **In 3D, geometry costs nothing** — 204 triangles, 27 draw calls: this really is a 1995 game. All
  of the cost is *per pixel*: 2.6 Mpx against 0.077 on the Amiga, with 14-light lighting. The only
  effect that pushed past the frame budget was **full-resolution bloom**; computing it at quarter
  resolution makes it free without changing how it looks.

---

## What works

- **Levels chain together**: title screen, menu, story screens, the full campaign driven by the
  original script, checkpoints and resume ("CONTINUE FROM…").
- **Movement and collision** following the asm's rules (sliding along walls, crushing), all five
  weapons firing with their own damage, rates and sounds.
- **AI per type**: marine, baldy, terra, ghoul, phantom, demon, lizard, troll — each with its
  original logic (charge, fire, dodge). Bosses: the dragon (circling plus homing missiles) and the
  deathhead (soul suck, which drags the player towards it).
- **Full gore**: impact sparks, 24 blood drops *on every hit taken*, gibs with gravity, persistent
  floor decals, a splat on the view when a drop grazes the camera.
- Monsters **flinch** when hit: stunned and untouchable for a moment.
- **Powerups**: weapon, thermo, invisibility, "hyper" invincibility, bouncy bullets, with their
  timers, their messages and their expiry warnings.
- **Dynamic geometry**: doors, rotating polygons, texture animations, trigger zones (ambushes,
  teleports, exit).
- **Audio**: every effect, the monsters' ambient voices, and the MED music.
- **3D view**: dynamic lighting (torch, muzzle flash, bullets), optional HD textures, thermal vision
  through walls, a persistent options menu, remappable controls.
- **Android**: a single APK with both renderers, touch controls, assets fetched on first run.

## What's missing

- **2-player mode** (serial modem link) and the chat — out of scope, like the rest of `ap.s`.
- The **Defender mini-game** (`combatok`).
- The music volume fade between levels (`fadevol`).
- Hit sounds are faithful, but a few monsters' **ambient voices** still need checking in situ.
- `ob_infra`: a leftover from the original — the "infrared" bonus actually hands you the thermo
  goggles, and the variable is never read anywhere. Reproduced as is.

---

## Running the game

### From source

You need the asset repository **next to** this one (the assets aren't redistributable, see below):

```
Gloom/
├── GloomAmiga/     ← git clone https://github.com/earok/GloomAmiga
└── gloom-java/
    └── java/       ← this Gradle project
```

Then, from `java/`:

```bash
gradle run                        # full game (2D / 3D launcher)
gradle run2                       # the gloom2.s variant (focshft 7 + castrots128)
gradle rebirth                    # straight into the 3D view
gradle run -Dscale=4              # bigger window (320×240 internally)
gradle run -Dmap=map1_3 -Dtile=1  # a single level (testing / sightseeing)
```

Options: `-Dw= -Dh= -Dscale= -Dmap= -Dtile= -Dengine=gloom2 -Dmedspeed= -Dgloom.assets=`.

**Requirements**: JDK 21 (the Gradle toolchain is pinned to it, and `jpackage` comes from it),
Gradle 9.x. The LWJGL natives are set to Windows x64; for Linux/macOS, change `lwjglNatives` in
`build.gradle` and build **on the target platform**.

**Controls** — `W`/`S` or `↑`/`↓` forward/back, `A`/`D` strafe, `←`/`→` turn, left click / `Ctrl` /
`Space` to fire and confirm, `Esc` to quit. In 3D the mouse aims, and the keys are remappable in the
OPTIONS menu.

### Android

A single APK holds both renderers. **Left thumb**: forward, back, turn. **Right thumb**: strafe
(◀ ▶) and fire. **MENU button**, top right: steps back one level (game → menu → launcher → quit),
same as the back key.

Android 8.0 minimum. Assets are downloaded on first run (network needed that once only).

---

## How it's verified

There are no unit tests in the usual sense: the reference isn't a specification, it's an assembly
file. So each subsystem has its own **harness**, which replays a scenario and compares the behaviour
to what the asm describes. About thirty in total, all under `src/gloom/tools/`:

```bash
gradle checkLayout        # memory layout: every offset against the .s
gradle mathTest           # RNG, angles, calcangle
gradle mapTest            # map and texture loading
gradle goreTest           # blood, gibs, decals, flinch → gore.png
gradle monsterTest        # AI per monster type
gradle bossTest           # dragon and deathhead
gradle powerupTest        # powerups, messages, animated objects, soul suck
gradle medTest            # MED player → med1.wav
gradle levelRenderTest    # renders one frame of a real level → level.png
gradle rebirth -Dshot     # screenshot of the 3D view → rebirth.png
```

Each one prints `TOUT OK` or writes a demonstration PNG/WAV. `gradle tasks --group verification`
lists them all.

---

## Layout

| directory | contents |
|---|---|
| `src/gloom/` | the engine: `Mem`, `M68k`, `Render`, `Objects`, `Player`, `Map`, `Events`, `Sfx`, `MedPlayer`… |
| `src/gloom/host/` | the PC host layer (LWJGL): window, audio, game loop, HUD, menus, sequencer |
| `src/gloom/rebirth/` | the jMonkeyEngine 3D view |
| `src/gloom/data/` | the asm's `.data` sections: precomputed tables, `objinfo` |
| `src/gloom/tools/` | the verification harnesses |
| `android/` | the Android module (compiles `../src` as is) |
| `scripts/` | side tooling (AI upscaling of the textures for HD mode) |
| `dist/` | the asset-fetching scripts shipped with the package |

---

## Distribution

```bash
gradle jpackage           # self-contained native app → build/jpackage/Gloom/Gloom.exe (bundled JRE)
gradle jpackageInstaller  # native installer: .msi (needs WiX), .dmg, .deb
cd android && gradle assembleRelease    # Android APK
```

The package holds the executable, the JRE, the jars and **`fetch-assets.bat`/`.sh`** — but **not the
assets** (see below). The user runs the script once, then the game.

Ready-made binaries are on the
[releases page](https://github.com/guillaumemonet/gloom-java/releases).

---

## Licence and credits

*Gloom* is © **Black Magic Software**. The **original `.s`/`.bb2` sources are public domain** (see
the `GloomAmiga` repository) and are this port's reference.

The **assets** — graphics, sounds, maps — **are not**, and are **never redistributed** here: neither
the repository, nor the PC package, nor the APK contains them. They are fetched from
[earok/GloomAmiga](https://github.com/earok/GloomAmiga), a preservation repository, on first run.

Original engine: **Black Magic Software** (1995).
Java port: **Guillaume Monet**.

The port was carried out with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic): writing the translation code, the
verification harnesses and the instrumentation. The architectural decisions, the validation against
the original assembly and the result remain the author's own.

# Alone in the Dark — Amiga

An unofficial Amiga port of the 1994 Macintosh **Alone in the Dark 1.0** by
Infogrames and Interplay. Explore the mansion of Derceto as Edward Carnby or
Emily Hartwood, solving puzzles and surviving its creatures.

The port runs the original 68k game code with an Amiga implementation of the
Macintosh services it uses. Graphics use AGA bitplanes; music and effects use Paula.
The game runs through the ending and
returns to the title sequence. See the [coverage and limits](docs/testing.md#gameplay-coverage)
and [open work](docs/open-work.md) for the remaining investigations.

Current Amiga release: **0.92 (15.10.2026)**.

## Requirements and installation

- AGA Amiga, 68020 or better; **68040 or better strongly recommended**.
- **2 MB Chip RAM and 8 MB Fast RAM**; more Fast RAM permits more PRELOAD caching.
- WHDLoad 17+, Installer 43+, and a supported Kickstart 3.1 image with its RTB.
- 8 MB destination space and 24 MB temporary disk space.
- For direct AmigaOS launch on 68040/68060: run SetPatch with the matching
  CPU support library installed and both instruction and data caches enabled.
  The executable preserves the OS cache policy; WHDLoad manages its own policy.

Extract `AloneInTheDark-0.92.lha`, open its **Alone in the Dark Install** drawer
and run **Install**. Select the destination, temporary drawer and the
[AloneInTheDark.img_.sit StuffIt archive](https://www.macintoshrepository.org/download.php?id=5338).
Leave it compressed: the included helper extracts and verifies all 74 files.
Use a disk temporary drawer on an 8 MB machine.

Start the installed **AloneInTheDark** icon. The opening starts with Infogrames;
the standalone MACPLAY splash is omitted, while the book credits remain. Saved games live in `Saved Games`
and survive an in-place update. The installer's explicit **Remove** option
also deletes saved games. The game uses the normal **4 KB process stack**.

No original game code/data, Kickstart image or WHDLoad binary is distributed.
See [the release ReadMe](release/ReadMe) for supported ROM filenames and full
installation instructions.

## Controls

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Arrow keys | Move and turn |
| Shift + movement | Run |
| Enter | Action/inventory menu |
| Escape | Back/cancel where supported by the game |
| Space + direction | Perform the selected action |
| S / M | Toggle effects / music |
| Right-Amiga + S / O / Q | Save / Load / Quit normally |
| F10 | Immediate WHDLoad exit, bypassing normal game cleanup |

The port displays the 320×200 game viewport. The Mac menu bar and screen-size
chooser are suppressed; keyboard commands and the original engine interfaces
provide the reached game actions. In FS-UAE, disable keyboard joystick
emulation if it consumes the arrow keys; the supplied launchers do this.

## Building

The game uses `m68k-amiga-elf-gcc`, `elf2hunk` and vasm. The WHDLoad slave also
needs external WHDLoad SDK and Amiga NDK includes. Release packaging needs
Python 3, an LH5-capable LHa encoder and Lhasa's `lha` for independent validation.

```sh
. amiga/env.sh
make release
```

This builds `dist/AloneInTheDark-0.92.lha` without original game data. For a
standalone executable, use `make -C amiga`. Tool paths, environment overrides,
local data and emulator setup are in [development.md](docs/development.md).
The [testing guide](docs/testing.md) covers regression and release checks.
The [documentation index](docs/README.md) covers architecture and data formats.

## Credits and licensing

Alone in the Dark and its original assets belong to their respective copyright
holders. This is an unofficial fan port, not affiliated with or endorsed by them.
The compatibility runtime follows the Vette! port; framework and C2P provenance
are recorded with their source.

The standalone extraction helper is LGPL-2.1-or-later; see
[its license and provenance](tools/install-data/README.md).
That license applies to the helper only, not to the original game.

# Vette! — Amiga

An unofficial Amiga port of the 1991 Macintosh **Color VETTE! 1.02**, originally
published by Spectrum HoloByte / Sphere, Inc. Race a Corvette through San Francisco
against the clock and a computer opponent.

The port runs the original 68000 game code with an Amiga implementation of the
Macintosh services it uses. Graphics use native bitplanes and a hardware mouse
pointer; sound uses Paula. All four single-player courses are supported.
Network play is not supported.

## Requirements and installation

- PAL Amiga with a 68020 or better; **68030 or better and AGA recommended**.
- WHDLoad 17+, Kickstart 2.04+ on the host, and a supported Kickstart 3.1 image
  with its matching RTB file.
- The slave reserves 1 MB Chip RAM and 4.5 MB other RAM, including its ROM image.
  Allow extra memory for the host system and PRELOAD.
- Installer V43+, 3 MB destination space and 12 MB temporary space.

The release is `Vette-0.92.lha`. Open its **Vette! Install** drawer and run
**Install**. Select the destination, temporary drawer and your
`VETTE__1.02_and_extras.sit` archive. Leave that archive compressed; the included
helper extracts and validates the required data. Start the installed **Vette!** icon.

No original game code/data, Kickstart image or WHDLoad binary is distributed.
See [the release ReadMe](release/ReadMe) for supported ROM filenames and full
installation instructions.

## Controls

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Arrow keys | Accelerate, brake and steer |
| 1–6 | Select forward gear |
| 0 / R | Neutral / reverse |
| + / − | Shift up / down |
| A | Automatic shifting |
| Z | Horn |
| P | Pause/options |
| Control + left mouse button | Quit normally and save scores |
| F10 | Immediate WHDLoad quit; pending scores are not saved |

Select a gear before accelerating. In FS-UAE, disable keyboard joystick
emulation if it consumes the cursor keys. More controls and game rules are in
[the playing guide](docs/manual.md).

## Building

The game uses `m68k-amiga-elf-gcc`, `elf2hunk` and vasm. The WHDLoad slave uses
external WHDLoad SDK and Amiga NDK includes; release packaging needs Python 3
and an LH5-capable LHa encoder.

```sh
. amiga/env.sh
make dist
```

This builds `dist/Vette-0.92.lha` without original game data. Tool paths, tests
and local emulator setup are documented in [development.md](docs/development.md).
The [documentation index](docs/README.md) covers architecture and data formats.

## Credits and licensing

VETTE! and its original assets belong to their respective copyright holders.
This is an unofficial fan port, not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

The standalone extraction helper is LGPL-2.1-or-later; see
[its license and provenance](tools/install-data/README.md).
That license applies to the helper only, not to the original game.

# Donald’s Alphabet Chase — DOS

Recovered C and handwritten assembly for retail `DONALD.EXE` and the alternate
extensionless `DONALD`. Both editions share one source tree; the alternate uses
`DONALD_ALT`, not a duplicate implementation. Correct source behavior takes
priority over matching the original instruction encoding.

## Setup

Use Python 3.11+, separately installed pinned Turbo C 2.0 compiler/linker,
large-model startup/runtime and headers, the qualified Linux x86-64 NASM closure,
and DOSBox-X. Exact identities are in `tools/toolchain.json` and `tools/runtime.json`.
No proprietary tools or original game media are distributed here.

Obtain `jdelezenne/re-tools` at immutable revision
`778cce71a58b3dddc7fa83dabf789fdf88bd8b66` outside this checkout. The required
shared files are individually pinned in `tools/project.json`. Setup locates
installed dependencies; it does not download tools or run the game.

```sh
python3 tools/setup.py --re-tools /external/re-tools \
  --tools /external/tc2 --tools /external/nasm-host \
  --dosbox /external/dosbox-x --work-root /external/donald-work
```

Settings go in ignored `tools/local.json`. Tools, original media, generated work,
captures and runtime copies stay external. Later commands work offline.

## Build and compare

```sh
python3 tools/build.py
python3 tools/recmp.py --program retail --reference /external/original/DONALD.EXE
python3 tools/recmp.py --program alt --reference /external/original/DONALD
```

Build compiles 27 C and eight ASM units per edition with genuine vendor startup
and one shared 1,024-byte raw font. It builds both products by default;
`--program retail` or `--program alt` selects one. Source-build regression identities:

| Edition | Work-root output | Bytes | SHA-256 |
| --- | --- | ---: | --- |
| retail | `retail/DONALD.EXE` | 55,512 | `86a853004e8e27bcfc195d47dfa13710d1cdcbd24439c61ac52eb65536ab2d5d` |
| alt | `alt/DONALD` | 55,432 | `9438b79a9ecb24ece9dcbc9680c31584f7b484a2f5c189e05029db2c9339fa4d` |

These intentionally differ from the supplied releases: 588 ordinary same-operation
register instructions replace matching-only byte encoders, changing 1,071 bytes
per edition. Headers, ordered relocations and all other image bytes are unchanged.
Real owner labels replace fixed paragraph biases, local graphics CS bases and a
cross-object scratch-address shortcut; no padding or binary patch is used. See [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) for bounds.

Build never reads an original executable, imports `agents/`, patches its output,
executes it or falls back to stale objects. The alternate native MZ output is
sealed unchanged under its actual extensionless release filename. Compiler timing
remains the default; no unmeasured speed setting is applied to this title.

`recmp.py` verifies the current source-build receipt and compares the whole raw
file: exit 0 identical, 1 different, 2 invalid/error. The supplied originals give
**exit 1**, as expected. Comparison neither rebuilds nor normalizes differences;
byte equality is not a veto on faithful source.

## Run

Provide the 27 genuine `.CMP` resources pinned in `tools/resources.json`:

```sh
python3 tools/run.py --game /external/donald-resources --fresh-runtime
python3 tools/run.py --program alt --game /external/donald-resources --fresh-runtime
```

Each command verifies and stages only its selected built edition and copied
resources in a distinct fresh external runtime. The DOS launch name is
`DONALD.EXE`; the alternate release artifact remains `DONALD`, with identical
bytes. Run requires no original executable, implicit build or other edition’s
build product. Omit `--fresh-runtime` to reuse the owned persistent copy.
Ordinary resource loading is read-only: no save directory or generated files are
declared, and undeclared runtime writes are rejected. Gameplay stays normal-core,
fixed 3,000 cycles; the runtime profile is not a compilation-speed setting.

Both newly built editions passed bounded EGA startup, title and living-room letter
interaction runs through these commands, with natural host return and unchanged
resources. This is not a full playthrough or an audible-fidelity test.

## Layout and limits

- `src/DONALD.EXE/`: source and adjacent headers shared by both actual outputs.
- `data/DONALD.EXE/`: the shared unchanged raw font, with per-edition image pins.
- `tools/`: exactly four identical shared scripts—setup, build, recmp, run—and
  necessary declarative inputs only.
- `agents/`: optional research/history, never an ordinary-command dependency.

The writable font workspace, original keyboard overreads/vector corruption,
unclamped DAC reads and cross-segment aliases remain intact. The mnemonic proof
covers established ordinary entry/consumer paths, not arbitrary corrupted state
or interior entry. GFX DATA-frame/physical-adjacency obligations and script/tune/palette ownership
remain explicit work. This is not complete semantic recovery, all-mode safety,
a full playthrough or an audible-fidelity claim.

skortscheff-corncob3d-readme-md.text:
# Corncob 3-D — Windows port

A C++17 / SDL2 port of **Corncob 3-D**, the early-90s DOS flight and combat game by Kevin Stokes, built from its
original MASM source (the `*.ASM` / `*.INC` files in this directory). The flight model, the 3D engine, the enemies and the
mission logic are translated routine by routine from the assembly, keeping its fixed-point arithmetic and quirks. The menu
programs of the original (MOAG, TOWER, ISCORE) have no source, so the front end is rebuilt from their text and the manual.

## Status

Everything in the plan is in and plays: title sequence and music, menus, pilots and careers, training and combat missions in
the four shipped theaters, AdLib sound, the control tower, the end-of-mission pictures and the lost-in-space sequence.
`docs/PORT_PLAN.md` has the phase by phase record, the deliberate deviations and what was left out.

Not done: several airfields per theater (the original supports nine, the shipped theaters have one), printing the
documentation. The raw-score weights, rank thresholds and medal rules are recreations; only the
three score examples of the manual are original.

## Project status: an experiment, unsupported

This started as a weekend experiment. It comes **with no support whatsoever**: no promised bug fixes, no roadmap, no
guarantee that issues or pull requests will be answered. It will probably never be called a finished project. It works and
it is fun to play, but expect rough edges.

**Please take it and run with it.** The code is MIT licensed, and the work done so far is a foundation anyone can build on:
copy it, fork it, rewrite parts of it, port it to other platforms, fix what bothers you, add what you miss. You don't need
to ask permission or send anything back. Ideas that would be welcome in a fork:

- several airfields per theater (the original supports nine)
- Linux and macOS builds, tested
- more faithful scoring, ranks and medals (the current rules are recreations)
- joystick support, demo recording and playback
- anything else you can think of

If you make something good out of it, I'd love to hear about it, but that is entirely optional.

## Requirements

| | |
|---|---|
| **OS** | Windows 10/11 (the only platform built and tested). The code has no Windows-specific calls, so Linux and macOS should build with the same CMake steps, but that is untried. |
| **Compiler** | Any C++17 compiler. Tested with GCC from MSYS2 UCRT64. |
| **Tools** | CMake 3.16 or newer, Ninja (or any CMake generator), git |
| **Library** | SDL2 (development package) |
| **CPU / GPU** | Modest. The game is software-rendered at 640x350 (the original EGA mode), so no GPU features are needed. Any PC from the last 10-15 years should do; I have not measured minimums. A higher `--hd` factor and the 60 fps default cost more CPU. |
| **RAM / disk** | Well under 100 MB of RAM; the source, build and game data together are a few hundred MB at most. |
| **Input** | Keyboard (the original keys, rebindable), or an Xbox-style gamepad. |
| **Audio** | Any sound output. The AdLib chip is emulated in software. |
| **Game data** | The original Corncob 3-D shareware files, which you supply (see below). |

## Quick start (Windows)

1. **Install MSYS2** from <https://www.msys2.org>. Open the **MSYS2 UCRT64** shell and run once:

   ```sh
   pacman -S --needed mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-cmake mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-ninja mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-SDL2 git
   ```

2. **Get the code.**

   ```sh
   git clone https://github.com/skortscheff/Corncob3D.git
   cd Corncob3D
   ```

3. **Build** (in the same UCRT64 shell, or in PowerShell after `$env:PATH = "C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin;$env:PATH"`):

   ```sh
   cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
   cmake --build build
   ```

4. **Add the game data** (see below), then **run** `build/corncob3d.exe`.

5. **Check it works** (optional): `ctest --test-dir build`. All 13 suites should pass in a few seconds with the game data in place. Without it, the
   suites that need the data are reported as skipped.

To make a folder you can zip and hand out: `cmake --build build --target package` writes `build/dist/Corncob3D`
(the exe, `SDL2.dll` and this README).

**On Linux or macOS** (untested): install a C++17 compiler, CMake, Ninja and the SDL2 development package from your
package manager, then run steps 2-4 above.

If the build fails, check that `cmake` finds SDL2 (`find_package(SDL2)`); on MSYS2 that means building from the UCRT64
shell, not the plain MSYS shell.

## Game data

**You need the original game files to play, but not to build.** The code compiles, and the program builds, without them;
the files are read when the game runs. Only the tests that fly or load real game content need them too, and without them
those tests are reported as skipped. So build in any order, but add the data before you run the game.

The data files are **not** in this repository, because they are copyrighted. Obtain the Corncob 3-D **shareware release**
yourself (the original distribution, as a zip) and extract it so that this file exists:

```
assets/original/IMG/3D.IMG
```

The extracted folder should look like the shipped game: `IMG/`, `DEF/` (the theaters `DUSK`, `MORNING`, `WASTELND`,
`WHTSANDS`), `VGA/`, `THT/`, the music files (`*.ROL`, `CCMUSIC.BNK`), `3.ADL` (the AdLib sound data), the text documents
(`CORNCOB.DOC` and others), and so on. You can also copy the original `3.EXE` and the other programs along with the rest;
the port does not run them.

**Where the game looks.** The exe looks for `assets/original/IMG/3D.IMG` starting in its own folder and then in up to five
parent folders, and also relative to the folder you launch it from. That is why `build/corncob3d.exe` finds the data in the
repository's own `assets/original/`, and why a packaged copy works with the data placed in an `assets/original` folder next
to the exe (`cmake --build build --target package` creates that folder with a note in it).

**Keep it out of git.** `assets/original/` is listed in `.gitignore`. Please don't commit or redistribute those files
through this repository.

**If the game won't start properly,** the usual cause is missing data. Check that `assets/original/IMG/3D.IMG` exists
in one of the places above. (The port does not yet show a friendly "game data not found" message.)

## How this port came about

I played Corncob 3-D as a kid on my DOS PC, and recently stumbled upon it again. Around the same time I enrolled in a
Claude certification course, and this project grew out of that: a chance to put what I was learning to work on a game
I had never forgotten.

Corncob 3-D (1991-92, Pie in the Sky Software / MVP Software) was written in 8086 assembly for DOS, talking straight to
EGA/VGA hardware, the AdLib chip and the PC keyboard interrupt. Its author later released the source, and it survived on
the Wayback Machine and a public GitHub mirror (see `NOTICE.md`). The source is a snapshot that does not match the shipped
`3.EXE` exactly, and the menu programs and the author's `sas.lib` were never part of it.

The port was done over about five days (14-18 October 2026) as a pair-programming project between a human and Claude Code, an AI
coding assistant, working from a written plan of ten phases. The key decisions:

- **Translate, don't rewrite.** Each assembly routine became a C++ routine with the same name, order and fixed-point
  arithmetic, quirks included. A build-time tool (`tools/asmdata`) reads the assembly's data definitions and generates the
  original data segment, so the translated code keeps working on the same memory layout.
- **Emulate the hardware, not the PC.** EGA bit planes, the AdLib chip (through the ymfm emulator), and the keyboard
  interrupt are emulated, rather than running the original code in an x86 emulator.
- **Test against the original.** The shipped `3.EXE` ran in DOSBox as a reference, and the tests replay flights over the
  theaters, check arithmetic against the 8086 behavior, and drive the menus end to end.
- **Rebuild what was missing.** The menu programs, high-score tables and tower screens were recreated from their text
  data and the manual.
- **Modernize gently.** A 60 fps time base that keeps the original's feel, an HD scale option, a modern instrument panel
  (`--classic-panel` restores the original), key rebinding and gamepad support.

`docs/PORT_PLAN.md` is the full phase-by-phase record, including every place where the port deliberately differs from the
original.

## Playing

Run `corncob3d.exe`. The title sequence plays (any key skips it), then the main menu: arrow keys and Enter, or the
highlighted letter. `Training missions` is the quick way into a plane; `Duty roster` makes a pilot whose career is kept
(pilots, theaters, high score lists and settings live in your user data folder; `--save-dir` changes it).

The flight keys are those of `CORNCOB.DOC` (keypad 8/2 nose down/up, 4/6 roll, 7/9 or z/x rudder, keypad +/- throttle,
space guns, c missiles, b bomb, e eject, F1 boss screen, F2 the control tower's missions, F4 help ...). They can be changed
in `keyboard/Joystick setup` > `reDefine keys`. An Xbox-style gamepad works as well: left stick flies, right stick looks, `A` guns,
`X` missiles, `B` bomb, `Y` flaps, `Back` eject, `Start` options menu (on foot: left stick walks, right stick looks). The pad also
works in every menu and screen: D-pad or left stick moves, `A` or `Start` is Enter, `B` or `Back` is Escape.

The simulation runs at 60 frames per second by default (a reworked time base keeps flight, weapons and timers at the original's pace);
`keyboard/Joystick setup` switches to the original's 20 and sets the high-resolution factor and smoothing. The same menu opens
during a flight with `Start` on a gamepad; it ends with `Return to the game` and `Return to the main menu`.

### Command line

```
--skip-intro  --no-music  --nosound  --hd <n>  --smooth | --no-smooth  --fps <n>  --classic-panel  --save-dir <dir>
```

and for looking at one thing (the full list is at the top of `src/main.cpp`): `--theater <name>` / `--training` fly a mission
directly, `--screenshot <bmp> --frames <n> --keyscript "<frame>+<hex>;..."` run one unattended, `--ui-keys` / `--ui-shots` drive the
menus unattended, `--fake-mission`, `--spawn-enemies`, `--end-pictures`, `--space-shot`, `--play-rol`, `--wav-rol`.

## Quality-of-life enhancements

Beyond a faithful port, a few things were added so it plays comfortably on a modern PC. Where it makes sense, they can be switched
back to the original behavior.

- **60 fps simulation.** The original ran at about 20 frames per second. The port runs at 60 by default, with flight,
  weapons and timers rescaled so the plane still handles like the original. 20 fps is available in
  `keyboard/Joystick setup` or with `--fps 20`.
- **Xbox-style gamepad.** Left stick flies, right stick looks around, `A` guns, `X` missiles, `B` bomb, `Y` flaps, `Back`
  eject, `Start` opens the options menu (`P` on the keyboard still pauses). On foot after ejecting, the left stick walks and strafes and the right stick looks.
  The pad also drives every menu and screen: D-pad or left stick moves (and repeats), `A`/`Start` is Enter, `B`/`Back` is Escape,
  `X` is Space, `LB`/`RB` are page up/down. Pilot names are typed with up/down (letter), right (next) and left (delete).
- **HD scaling.** Missions can be drawn at 1x to 4x the original 640x350 (`--hd <n>` or the setup menu), keeping the EGA look.
- **Smoothing (anti-aliasing).** From 2x up, the larger picture is filtered down to the window instead of being stretched pixel by
  pixel, which softens the jagged edges (`--no-smooth` or the setup menu turns it off). 3x or 4x gives the best result; at 1x the
  pixels stay sharp.
- **Modern instrument panel.** Anti-aliased dials, lamps and bars over the EGA picture. `--classic-panel` restores the
  original panel.
- **Rebindable keys.** `keyboard/Joystick setup` > `reDefine keys`; bindings are saved in your settings.
- **Persistent pilots and settings.** Careers, high scores and options are kept in your user data folder
  (`--save-dir` changes it).
- **No DOS setup needed.** No `CONFIG.SYS` tweaking, no sound card IRQs, no CPU-speed throttling. It runs in a normal
  window, and AdLib sound and music are emulated.

## Layout

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `*.ASM`, `*.INC`, `*.LNK`, `MAKEFILE` | Original source (the game exe is linked per `3S.LNK`, shareware) |
| `tools/asmdata/` | MASM data-segment extractor (build-time code generator); `tools/theaterstats` counts objects |
| `src/core/` | Bit-exact equivalents of the original arithmetic (`AsmMath`), the author's library routines (`SasLib`) |
| `src/engine/` | The 3D engine: `F3dVec`, `F3dObj` (collisions, object calls), tables |
| `src/game/` | The game: `GameState` (the original data segment), `Main3*` (the main loop, flight, weapons, enemies), `World`, `Keyboard`, `Inst`, `MissionRunner`, `TheaterFiles` |
| `src/audio/` | `Opl` (ymfm chip), `Sound` (the AdLib effects), `RolPlayer` (the music) |
| `src/render/`, `src/platform/` | EGA screen emulation, frame buffer, SDL window and input |
| `src/ui/` | Title and story, text screens, the menus (`FrontEnd`), pilots and scores (`Career`, `Scoring`), tower screens, mission-end pictures |
| `tests/` | ctest suites |
| `docs/PORT_PLAN.md` | The plan, what was done, deviations and what was left out |

## Notes on fidelity

- Arithmetic follows the 8086 code, including quirks (sign tests after `cmp`, 16-bit wraps, `rand_w` is a stand-in generator
  since `sas.lib` is not in the source). Divide overflows saturate where the 8086 would trap.
- The source tree is a later snapshot than the shipped `3.EXE`: it is built as `guns=1`, `slalom=0`, `getunivbin=0`.
- Decisions where the original is unclear or buggy are listed in `docs/PORT_PLAN.md`.

## License and credits

- The port's code (`src/`, `tests/`, `tools/`, `docs/`, build files) is **MIT licensed** — see `LICENSE`. Contributions are welcome.
- The original assembly source in the repository root is by Kevin Stokes / Pie in the Sky Software. Its author publicly
  permitted free use of it; it is not relicensed here. Source: the [foone/Corncob3D](https://github.com/foone/Corncob3D)
  mirror, originally released in 2001 ([Wayback snapshot](https://web.archive.org/web/20020108042105/http://psky.com/prog/downloads.htm)).
- [ymfm](https://github.com/aaronsgiles/ymfm) (BSD 3-Clause, © Aaron Giles) emulates the AdLib chip; SDL2 (zlib) handles window, input and audio output.
- Corncob 3-D is © 1991-92 Pie in the Sky Software / MVP Software; the music is © James L. Collymore. This repository holds
  the port's code, not the game's data, which you must supply yourself.

Full details, including what is deliberately not included, are in `NOTICE.md`. This is an unofficial fan project, not
affiliated with the original authors or publisher.
